Repeated reference to @HEBobiwine as ‘kabobi’ by @mkainerugaba seems to have given license to many Ugandans to denigrate him conveniently forgetting that he succeeded in the cutthroat music industry in Uganda and the even more cutthroat politics industry as a former MP and current party leader.  Most of the people denigrating him have never led a football team or even a household. 

Some notable examples from Grok of presidents (or equivalent heads of state) who were widely seen as not looking, seeming, or acting particularly “presidential” before their election or rise to power. These individuals often came from unconventional, humble, entertainment, or non-elite backgrounds that clashed with traditional expectations of gravitas, polish, formal experience, or statesmanlike demeanor.
1Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (Brazil, elected 2002) A former factory worker, union leader, and shoeshine boy who had little formal education (he left school early and was illiterate until his teens). Many in Brazil’s political and media elite mocked his rough working-class origins, strong regional accent, and lack of elite polish or university credentials. He was frequently dismissed as too unrefined or “unpresidential” for the office, yet he won as an anti-establishment figure promising change for the poor.
2George Weah (Liberia, elected 2017) A world-famous soccer star and African Footballer of the Year who had no prior political experience. Before running, he was known purely as an athlete and celebrity, with critics arguing he lacked the education, policy knowledge, or sophisticated bearing expected of a head of state. Many viewed him as a celebrity outsider playing at politics rather than a serious statesman, but his popularity as a national hero carried him to victory.
3Jimmy Morales (Guatemala, elected 2015) A comedian and TV personality famous for slapstick humor and a folksy, anti-establishment persona. He had zero political background and campaigned with the slogan “I’m not corrupt, I’m not a thief.” His informal, joke-heavy style and lack of traditional gravitas led many to see him as unserious or unqualified for the presidency — the ultimate outsider who surprised the political class by winning amid widespread anti-corruption anger.
4Joseph Estrada (Philippines, elected 1998) A popular action-movie star and former mayor who built his fame playing tough-guy roles in films. Before his presidency, he was often seen as a showbiz figure rather than a credible leader — critics highlighted his lack of elite education, folksy mannerisms, and Hollywood background as making him seem far from presidential. His win reflected voter appeal to his everyman image over traditional political figures.
5Nayib Bukele (El Salvador, elected 2019) A millennial businessman and former ad executive who projected a casual, social-media-savvy, non-traditional image (often in baseball caps, jeans, and using memes). Before politics, he lacked conventional political credentials or gravitas, and many dismissed him as a flashy, inexperienced outsider more focused on branding than substance. His unconventional style and anti-establishment vibe shocked the old guard but resonated with voters.

6. Volodymyr Zelenskyy (Ukraine, elected 2019) A comedian and actor who played the president in a popular TV sitcom. Before running, he had no political experience and was known for entertainment rather than serious statesmanship. His informal style, humor, and lack of traditional political demeanor made him seem the antithesis of a conventional head of state — yet he won in a landslide as an anti-establishment outsider.

These leaders often turned their “unpresidential” traits — informality, outsider status, entertainment roots, or humble origins — into strengths, appealing to voters frustrated with traditional politicians. This pattern appears in various regions, especially where anti-elite sentiment runs high.
